To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of glucose production decreases during the fast but remains similar to that of the postabsorptive state, the fractional contributions of glycogenic precursors did not change with the fast and PEP was the major gluconeogenic precursor, and fluxes through the TAC cycle, PEP carboxykinse, and pyruate cycling were higher in elephant seals than other species.

northern elephant seals maintain a high rate of glucose production during their natural postweaning fast by increasing the rate of gluconeogenic PEP production and recycling PEP through a high rate of pyruvate and TCA cycle flux.
the rate of glucose production in elephant seals decreases with fasting but remains similar to that of mammals in postabsorptive states.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolic adaptations that allow elephant seals to sustain a high metabolic rate while undergoing prolonged periods of fasting.
the metabolic adaptations that allow elephant seals to survive prolonged periods of fasting while maintaining high levels of activity.

the regulation of glucose metabolism in fasting elephant seals and how these animals meet the demands of their glucose-dependent tissues during prolonged periods of fasting while maintaining high levels of activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

elephant seals maintain high rates of glucose production during fasting through the use of gluconeogenic precursors derived from pyruvate, which is generated by pyruvate dehydrogenase, a reaction that is highly regulated and energetically costly.
the metabolic pathways of elephant seals are highly active and that they have evolved to meet the metabolic needs of glucose-dependent tissues during long fasts while maintaining protein sparing.
elephant seals have evolved a unique and efficient strategy to maintain glucose production during fasting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

elephant seals are capable of suppressing gluconeogenesis and protein catabolisms while fasting and that the high rates of pyruvate and TCA cycling in elephant seals are associated with the high rates of gluconeogenesis and PEP production.

northern elephant seals are able to maintain high rates of energy metabolism while fasting by suppressing protein breakdown and maintaining rates of glucose synthesis similar to postabsorptive species, but at the cost of increased flux through TCA and PEPCK.

the high rate of pyruvate and TCA fluxes in elephant seals is likely an adaptation to the high rate of gluconeogenesis that is necessary to maintain high rates of glucose-dependent tissue metabolism in this fasting-adapted mammal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
elephant seals are able to produce glucose at rates comparable with postabsorptive animals by increasing gluconeogenic fluxes rather than increasing gluconeogenic precursor supply.

northern elephant seals are able to meet their glucose needs during prolonged fasts while maintaining high levels of activity without substantial loss of protein by using PEP as a gluconeogenic precursor.
elephant seals maintain high rates of energy expenditure and activity during fasting by maintaining high rates of gluconeogenesis and TCA cycling while suppressing protein crosstalk.
